Well, here we are back from our little Christmas holiday break. If you are
like me, pretty much everything is put on at least semi-hold due to all the
interruptions. Consequently not much turning came out of my shop during
the last month. For me, that resulted in a couple of things.
First, since turning is a hand-eye and muscle-memory thing, my tool
control kind of went in the tank. Normally, whenever I start turning for the
day I either throw a sacrificial piece between centers and turn some beads
and coves or if a project is still in the lathe I’ll have left enough material
to make some practice cuts just to get back in the game. As I always say,
turning is no different than playing a musical instrument: you must practice
your (wood turning) scales every day to keep the muscles in tune. Having
missed a few weeks of steady turning I needed a much longer session at
that and actually enjoyed just making shavings with no particular design or
size constraints involved. That was fun. The morale: if you feel like turning
but don’t have anything in mind - just go make stuff.
What wasn’t nearly as much fun was that I also kind of lost my
motivation and direction. That was partly due to the fact that over the
last year and a half I had been preparing for my solo gallery show in
November. All my focus was on that event with no real plans beyond. The
show sent me in a new direction but now I’m a bit at loose ends with no
particular goals. Once back in the shop I did some minor organizing that
had been on my mind but finally had to face my demons. One thing that I
have learned over time is that ideas come far easier when you are actually
turning, either from “design opportunities” or from rambling “what-ifs”. I
took the bull by the horns, threw a giant piece of not-so-good wood in
the lathe and started making shavings. Between feeling good, having fun
shooting shavings at various targets and making shapes that really didn’t
matter if they made sense, I loosened the bolts that had a tight hold on my
brain and the ideas started to flow. Second morale: same as the first – just
go out and turn.
The down side of all that of course is the sweeping-up part, but the
satisfaction level is through the roof – even though I didn’t really make
anything.
Don’t forget the January President’s challenge will be a finial (don’t even
need the box to go with it) or some other similar small, finely-detailed
piece turned between centers. February’s will be “Unsanded”, as in “no
sandpaper allowed”.
January’s President’s Challenge
“Finials or turning between 2 centers.”
February’s President’s Challenge
“Unsanded - No sand paper allowed!”

Look Who is Coming to Demonstrate in March
Peter McLaren
￼
photo from Glenn Lucas Studio - Ireland
Mark your calendar for the March 16, Ashley
Harwood’s Demo Day and March 17th Hands on
Class.
This young artist is rapidly making a name for
herself both at various turning centres around the
world and on the professional demonstration circuit.
Check out her web site at
http://www.ashleyharwood.net/ashleyharwood/
Woodturning.html
Ashley will demonstrate how she creates the
delicate spindles she attaches to her sea urchin
ornaments. This is done with three tools: the bowl
gouge, detail gouge and the vortex tool, which I
understand is an adaptation of Cindy Drozda’s
custom point tool. Ashley will demonstrate the
cutting and sharpening techniques for each tool,
explaining the particular qualities that enable her to
make successful cuts. All of her sharpening is done
only with a platform.
She will demonstrate how that grind helps her
shape the outside and inside of her bowls, showing
us how she makes one continuous cut on the
outside of the bowl with no torn grain. Ashley will
also be demonstrating thin bowl turning, using the
“push cut” technique. For all finish cuts she will use
the same/40 grind bowl gouge that she uses in her
fine spindle turning.
The differences between the various flutes shapes
and the sharpening subtleties will be explained
along with her Seven Fundamentals of Woodturning.
Ashley started turning when her father enrolled
both of them in a weeklong class in turning bowls.
Once bitten by the turning bug she benefitted
tremendously through an apprenticeship with
Stuart Batty, where she learned about the 40/40
grind and the push cut. He subsequent success
as an instructor is proof that good lessons pay high
dividends.
Whether you have been turning for several years
or consider yourself a complete novice, I believe
that every guild member could benefit to some
extent from the demo and more so from the class
that Ashley is teaching. While Ashley has proposed
a 2 day session to cover all the basics, the response
so far suggests we may only have interest for a
one day session. That hands on class will cover
fundamental cuts in spindle turning, freehand
sharpening, and the push cut on shaping the outside
of bowls
My name is first on the list of members signed
up for her class, let me know on Wednesday if you
have paid your registration amount to the treasurer
to join me.
The cost of all hands on classes is $160 per
day. This class will be held at Island Woodcraft in
Coquitlam.
Once I know who all is in the class I will confirm
the tools you should bring.
Peter McLaren mclaren47@shaw.ca

Jimmy Clewes is Coming to Demonstrate in May
Peter McLaren
As self described,
“Jimmy is not your
ordinary woodturner.
Upon a first meeting
one would think of
him as a renegade,
a free thinker and
not within the
stereotypical image
of a woodturner.
His charming British
style, unending
wit, creative mind
and magnetic personality are only some of the
attributes that make him popular in the woodturning
demonstration circuit. Jimmy is on the Register of
Professional Woodturners in the United Kingdom
and a member of the American Association of
Woodturners. He has over 22 years of experience in
woodturning and woodworking. The demand for his
services as a freelance demonstrator and teacher
takes him all over the world including his homeland
of the United Kingdom, Europe, Canada, Norway,
Finland, New Zealand, Belgium, Australia.”
On Saturday, May 4th at Sapperton Hall, Jimmy
Clewes will be demonstrating his;
•
Basic Bowl turning,
•
Coloured Rim Platter,
•
Long Long Stem Goblet,
•
Natural Edge end-grain vase, wet turned, and
•
Arabic Box.
Check out some shots from an earlier demo
in Barrier Ont.: http://simcoewoodturnersguild.
com/2011/10/jimmy-clewes-full-day-demonstration/
Jimmy is prepared to run 2 one day sessions with
2 different projects on each day - including:
Coloured Rimmed Platter,
Natural-edged end-grain vase,
Square Oriental Box,
Oyster or Clam Shell box
I have one class scheduled for Friday, May 3rd., if
there is enough interest shown in advance, we can
add a Thursday session.
This link will give you an idea of one fellow’s
approach to Jimmy’s Oriental Box: http://
bobhamswwing.com/Articles/Clewes%20Style%20
Box/Clewes%20box%20Page%201.htm
The following tools are suggested by Jimmy for
his class sessions;
•
Bowl Gouge - 1/4”
•
Bowl Gouge - 3/8” or 1/2”
•
Spindle Roughing Gouge
•
Parting Tool
•
Round Nose Scraper
•
Spindle Gouge 3/8”
•
Screw Chuck
•
Sanding to 400 grit, Sanding sealer, wax,
Danish - Deft oil or similar.
You can learn more about Jimmy Clewes from his
web site at http://www.jimmyclewes.com/clewes/
GeneralWebsite/AboutMe.aspx?Feature=2
If you want to reserve your spot in Jimmy’s class,
let me know now so we can decide if we will run one
or two sessions. Each day of the hands-on class is
$160, payable to our treasurer.
email me at mclaren47@shaw.ca

Solving an impossible problem.
Bruce Campbell
Twelve members of the Guild got together on
Saturday, Jan 12 to help clean up and dispose of
the shop of Graham Hogarth, who passed away
suddenly last summer. Graham was a champion
wood scrounger and we took hundreds of pieces
of wood and dozens of pieces of equipment from
their various storage locations to be disposed.
About half of the wood went for firewood, another
large amount ended in the dumpster and the rest
was split amongst those who helped. Several folks
purchased various pieces of equipment while others
hauled away things that needed repair. In the end,
Lynda (Graham›s widow) ended up with a clean
yard, a clean garage, and a nice sum of money.
Those that helped out got lots of nice turning wood,
some firewood, and the reward of helping out a
family recovering from loss.
The Guild has been offering this estate clean-up
service for about 10 years. The big challenge is
that we all seem to have a habit of collecting things
that we never get to. It becomes a real problem for
the family when it comes to cleaning up. What is
a small piece of firewood to them is a $100 piece
of snakewood to us and that piece of bent steel is
an expensive hollowing bar to us. By helping out
we offer manpower, expertise, and a ready group
of consumers. What we give back is some cash, a
clean shop, and relief from a seemingly unsolvable
problem.
As part of our estate planning it is worth
considering how to deal with our shops when the
time comes. Some of us have family members who
will gladly take over our shops. But most of us leave
behind a huge, confusing mess for our loved ones.
A simple solution is to let everyone know that the
Guild can be called on to help out.
Thanks to all those that helped out in Graham›s
clean-up. Lynda asked me to pass on her sincere
thanks for all your help.
Rocco Says, “Thanks”
As some of you know, Rocco Cerenzie has
provided a lot of quality turning wood to many of
us and the only thing he asked in return was two
turned pieces from each of us. Those pieces were
collected for a charity auction held each December
with the proceeds going to the Children’s Hospital
in the name of “Emily”, a member of his daughter’s
basketball team. The auction brought in $9,443.00.
Rocco recently sent a message of thanks to our
guild as well as the Fraser Valley and Edmonton
guilds. Rocco writes:
“I would like at this time to thank each and
every one of you for your hard work and time
with your donations to the tournament for
Emily. Again it was a success, thanks to you
all. Please read the letter I received from the
coach of Riverside Secondary School tonight.
Without you all this could not be possible. We
at Specialty Craft Woods thank you fro your
support.
Roccino and Catherine Cerenzie”
The letter referred to is from Paul Langford,
coach of Riverside Secondary School in Coquitlam,
addressed to participants in the charity thanking
them for their contributions. It is a lengthy letter but
the section Rocco wanted us to see specifically
follows:
Thanks to Everyone in the Tournament for
Emily. Over the last decade or so, a number of
basketball girls fought a tough battle against
cancer. Each of those girls would rather have
been playing basketball, but there’s no doubt
that all them are pleased to be remembered
by the players who helped to raise the money
to buy a team donation for the silent auction.
These teams, the wood turners, sponsors and
others who supported the Tournament for
Emily helped to make life a little better for kids
undergoing cancer treatment at BC Children’s
Hospital.
Rocco noted that there were some turners who
didn’t want to have their names mentioned and he
would like them to know they are included in his
thanks.

Turning 101 November 2012
Cathy Friesen
At our November Turning 101 workshop Allan
Cusworth taught us how to turn a hanging Christmas
ornament using a spindle gouge. He also showed
us how to make our own wire hangers and to use
a pin vise to drill a very small hole in the top of the
ornament for the wire hanger.
In the afternoon Alan demonstrated the proper
use of a skew by turning a small standing Christmas
Tree.
Having the class held in the Instructional
Classroom at KMS Tools in Coquitlam gave us a
great opportunity to try out different lathes.
Thank you Allan, Gerry and
Kees for once again, sharing
your time and experience with
all of us.
Thank you too to KMS Tools
for supplying the venue and
equipment for our class.
Tentative dates for 2013 Turning 101 classes
In 2013 all classes will be held on the 2nd
Saturday of the month, 9:00 am- 4:00 pm at KMS
Tools in Coquitlam. Cost is $25 per session. All
equipment is supplied by KMS, bring your own tools.
Annual General Meeting
Ed Pretty
Our February meeting is the Annual General
Meeting. As such, we will be discussing some
housecleaning changes to our bylaws and
conducting elections.
You may recall from the November issue that
there are a few positions to be filled, notably four
Member at Large positions, Vice President and
the Treasurer’s position. I can’t stress enough
how important it is that we have input from newer
members as well as those who have been members
for a while. So far, we haven’t served anyone up
on a spit at any meetings. ☺ These positions
don’t require a lot of personal time and afford the
opportunity to contribute to the guild’s growth.
Meetings are held only every two months, except
during summer, and come complete with pizza
dinners.
Many times folks feel they aren’t suitable or
capable for positions when in reality they have a lot
to contribute. Please consider serving on the board
and if you know someone who is standing in the
wings that you feel would do well in a position, give
them a nudge and nominate them at the meeting.
In either case, feel free to approach any member of
the board to ask any questions that you may have.
If you don’t know who is a board member, check
the website. You will likely see a couple of familiar
names.

2013 Proposed amendments to the bylaws of the guild.
This is a notice given to members of the GVWG of proposed amendments to the Bylaws of the Guild.
In order to amend bylaws, a society must register the amendments with the Corporate Registry in Victoria.
If this is not done, then the bylaws changes are not valid. Unfortunately, in any society run by volunteers
this requirement is sometimes overlooked. This was the case with all of the bylaw amendments that the
GVWG made since incorporation. As such, the previously passed amendments are being proposed again.
If passed, the amendments will be filed in Victoria, making them valid.
In order to pass, 3/4 of the membership at the Annual General Meeting must vote in favour of the
changes.
The proposed amendments follow, with deletions struck out and additions highlighted. An explanation of
the reason for the change follows each proposed change.
1(a) Bylaws means the bylaws of a the society.
Explanation: The only bylaws referred to in the document are the bylaws of the GVWG. This language
is clearer.
2(d): The amount of the first annual membership dues must be determined by the directors and after that
the annual membership dues may only be altered at the annual general meeting of the society.
Explanation: The executive is responsible for running the Guild, and ensuring that it remains an
economically viable organization. Costs rise from time to time. Membership fees are paid in September,
and the AGM is in February. A vote to increase the fee will result in increased revenue the following
September. As such, the following could occur: a fee increase, such as the cost of renting the hall, could
occur in February, too late for a motion at the AGM. The motion to increase fees would have to wait until
the following February, and then take effect the following September, resulting in an 18 month delay before
expenses are balanced by revenue.
6(c): The president, past-president, vice president, secretary, treasurer and one or more up to six (6)
other persons are the directors of the society.
6(f): The president, and secretary and up to three (3) other persons are to be elected in even-numbered
years and the other directors vice-president, treasurer and up to three (3) other persons are to be elected in
odd-numbered years.
Explanation: Over the years the number of directors varied. At times the number was large, making
meetings unwieldy. It seems that about 10 directors provides a sufficiently wide breadth of experience,
and still remains a manageable number for meetings. The alternating years for elections are designed to
ensure that there is continuity in the board of directors. Formalizing the election of the Members at Large
in alternating years helps with this. Notwithstanding this, there have been occasions where most of the
board members have been recently elected, with little knowledge of what was done in the past, or why. The
creation of the past-president position is an attempt to improve continuity.
6(g): No director is to hold the same office for more than two consecutive terms. However, if a director is
elected or appointed to an office and serves less than 12 months before the next election for that position,
that time will not be counted as a term.
6(j): The directors may at any time and from time to time appoint a member as a director to fill a vacancy
in the directors. A director so appointed holds office only until the conclusion of the next annual general
meeting of the society, but is eligible for re-election at the meeting.
Explanation: In the past the directors have occasionally appointed a director mid-term to fill a position.
On other occasions a director has resigned one post to run for another (e.g. Vice President resigning to run
for President) and an election has been held ‘mid-term’ to fill the vacant post. Without an exception like this,
service of a couple of months would be the same as service for an entire two year term. Since no director
can serve more than two consecutive terms in the same office, such an individual would effectively be
limited to one term. Since the guild depends on volunteers, it is not in the best interests of the guild to limit

its volunteers in this way. The deletions from clause (j) are to make it consistent with the two year terms as
set out in clause (f).
6(k): If a director resigns his or her office or otherwise ceases to hold office, the remaining directors
must appoint a member to take the place of the former director. Notwithstanding sub-paragraph j, if the
President, Vice President, Secretary or Treasurer resigns his or her office or otherwise ceases to hold
office, the remaining directors must appoint a replacement.
Explanation: clauses (j) and (k) are contradictory. Clause (j) permits the directors to appoint somebody
to fill a vacancy. Clause (k) requires them to do this. The new clause (k) requires the directors to make
appointments to fill key officer roles, while maintaining the discretion to do so for other director position with
clause (j).
6(o) Notwithstanding any clauses in paragraph 6, the position of past president is an appointed position
held by the most recent past-president for a term of one year after his or her term as president has ended.
Explanation: As discussed above, this is to help with continuity while ensuring that past-presidents do
not outstay their welcome.
14(a): A notice may be given to a member, either personally, by mail to the member at the member’s
registered address or (if the member so chooses) by email to the member at the member’s email address.
Explanation: When the Guild was formed, few people had email. Now almost everybody has it. This
change will allow the Guild to deliver notices in the most cost effective manner possible.

FOR SALE
Jim Bain (604)-255-9729 is selling off his whole
woodworking shop of tools. The stationary tools
are all Craftsman and have little mileage on them.
They include a 14” bandsaw, 10” table saw, 17”
drill press , and a 6x48 belt sander. In addition
he has routers and laminate trimmers, a jigsaw,
and router bits. He also has quite a lot of book
matched veneers. He needs to sell everything and
is open to a package deal. Please contact Jim if
you are interested in more details.
Formal But Fun Turning Classes

Classes range from introductory to advanced
